newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian parties wrap up election campaigns.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian parties wrap up election campaigns.

text.p: Bulgaria's political parties on Thursday ended campaigning for parliamentary elections which will put their ex-communist country belatedly on the path of market reform.

The Union of Democratic Forces gathered thousands of supporters outside the Alexander Nevsky cathedral to sing the songs and chant the slogans of a month-long protest campaign that toppled the Socialist government in February.
"This is the last train. We are going to catch it together on April 19," said UDF leader Ivan Kostov.

"We shall seek consensus and we know that consensus is now reached on the need for financial discipline, the introduction of a currency board system, privatisation and the integration of the country into the European Union and NATO."
On the other side of the city, the ex-communist Socialists offered traditional folk music to a rather smaller, overwhelmingly elderly crowd outside the National Palace of Culture.

"By voting with the red ballot paper on April 19 we will say a decisive no to the restoration of the monarchy, no to returning the Saxe-Coburg dynasty to power," Socialist leader Georgi Parvanov told the crowd.
"We shall say yes to a republic and to dialogue and consensus in parliament, yes to active reform, but at an acceptable social price."
Exiled King Simeon visited Bulgaria on Tuesday and Wednesday and urged its political forces to unite in a broad coalition to carry out the long-delayed reforms.

President Petar Stoyanov said that if parliament were to vote for a referendum on restoring the monarchy, he would support it. His words were seized on by the Socialists, who had already accused the UDF of planning to bring back the king.
The election campaign has been something of an anti-climax after the UDF-led rallies which drew thousands of people every day at the beginning of the year.
Opinion polls suggest the UDF will get up to 60 percent of votes and the Socialists around 20 percent. Three smaller coalitions could poll above the four percent minimum to enter parliament.
Kostov, an economist by training and a former UDF finance minister, is expected to be prime minister.

He has capitalised on the success of the interim cabinet, which brought Bulgaria back from the brink of bankruptcy, negotiating a reform and funding accord with the IMF which opened the door to credits from other lenders.
The lev currency, which went into freefall at the beginning of the year, has now stabilised but the annual inflation rate reached 2,040.5 percent in March.
The jobless rate hit 14.5 percent and was expected to rise further as the government finally began closing or restructuring of loss-making state enterprises.
The new government will have to implement reforms agreed with the IMF, including introducing a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime in June to restore monetary stability.
Bulgaria stands to receive credits totalling $1.2 billion from the IMF, European Union and others, most of which must go straight back to lenders as payment on its foreign debt.
After former communist leader Todor Zhivkov was toppled in 1989, leading communists renamed their party the Bulgarian Socialist Party and stayed in government.
The UDF won parliamentary elections in 1991, but lost a no-confidence vote the following year.

The Socialists returned to power in elections in 1994, but their support evaporated as the economy weakened and Stoyanov decisively defeated of the Socialist candidate in presidential elections last year.
